opus-5.5.text:
I think it can, but probably not in the way most people expect.

When people talk about AI in education, the first picture is usually remediation: a student is falling behind, the AI explains the concept again, patiently, as many times as needed. That's real and valuable. But for students who already do well, the bottleneck is different. They usually aren't stuck on understanding the textbook. What limits them is that the system around them is built for the middle of the distribution. The class moves at a pace that's too slow, the problems are too routine, and the teacher, with forty students, simply doesn't have time to push one kid further.

So for a strong student, the most useful thing AI can be is a sparring partner rather than a tutor. You can ask it, "Why is this proof done this way and not another way?" or "What happens if I drop this assumption?" Those are the questions that used to require access to a really good mentor, a professor, an older sibling who did olympiad math. Most kids never had that. Now the barrier to asking a deep follow-up question at eleven at night is basically gone.

That said, there's a real risk, and it's actually higher for good students. They're efficient. They know how to get the answer. If the AI just hands them polished solutions, they'll get the grade with less struggle, and the struggle is exactly where the deeper ability comes from. Being good at school and being good at thinking start to diverge at some point, and AI can widen that gap if it's used as a shortcut.

So my honest answer: yes, it can help them go much further, maybe more than it helps anyone else, because they're the ones most able to ask good questions. But only if they treat it as something to argue with, not something to copy from. The tool amplifies whatever habit the student already has.

r001.rationale: The response says AI may help strong students go further and could let them get grades with less struggle, but it does not identify freed-up time for more productive activities as a benefit.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the top students are the ones AI helps the least, at least in the short term. A student who already gets good grades usually has the fundamentals in place: they know how to read a problem, they know how to check their own work, they have discipline. For them, AI is a convenience, maybe it saves some time looking things up. But the marginal gain is small.

Where it really changes things is for the student in the middle, or the one who is struggling, because what they are missing is often not intelligence, it is feedback. In a class of forty, the teacher cannot sit with each child and say, "Here is exactly where your thinking went wrong." AI can do that, patiently, at eleven at night, without judgment. That is a kind of attention that used to be available only to families who could afford tutors.

That said, for the strong students there is one thing AI can do that a classroom cannot. It can remove the ceiling. The curriculum is designed for the average, so a very capable kid often spends years being slightly bored. If they are curious, AI lets them go as deep and as far as they want, on their own schedule. So I would say AI does not make good students "better" in the sense of higher scores. It makes them freer. And whether that turns into something meaningful depends entirely on the kid's curiosity, not the tool.

r001.rationale: The response says AI may save strong students time looking things up and lets curious students explore further, but it does not identify AI completing their homework to free time for more productive activities.

astra-6.text:
Yes, I think it can. For students who already get good grades, the biggest benefit may be helping them go beyond getting the right answer. They can ask AI, “Is there another way to solve this?” or “What changes if we remove this assumption?” That can push them toward a deeper understanding.

AI can also quiz them, ask them to explain their reasoning, and help reveal gaps that a good test score might hide. But how they use it matters. If they simply ask for answers, they miss the opportunity to think. I’d encourage them to try a problem first, then use AI to challenge their approach—and remember that AI’s feedback can be wrong too.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using AI to deepen understanding, quiz the student, and challenge their reasoning. It does not identify freeing time for more productive activities as a benefit of AI completing homework.

sol-6.1.text: Yes, I think it can. Students who already get good grades don’t necessarily need more exercises; they may need deeper challenges. AI can help them explore different ways to solve a problem, question their assumptions, or connect ideas across subjects. For example, instead of asking AI for an answer, they could ask, “Where is my reasoning weakest?” or “How would this problem change if we removed this condition?” The key is to use AI to stretch their thinking while still doing the thinking themselves.

r001.rationale: The response describes using AI to deepen and stretch students’ thinking, but does not say that AI completing homework frees time for more productive activities.
